findings.checklist_item: Name the immediate consumer of get_parent_map and confirm the propagated RunawayPaginationError is surfaced/logged (not re-swallowed by another fail-open) — mirroring how acli_graph's readers handle the re-raise at 304-306.
evidence: M2: get_parent_map's 'except Exception: warn; return {}' previously converted aborts into a silent empty map; step 2 makes RunawayPaginationError propagate past it
Plan states 'another stream owns set_parent/parent handling' but does not name the caller that receives the propagated error or its handling behavior
findings.finding: The plan changes get_parent_map's degradation contract from 'return {} on any exception' to 'propagate RunawayPaginationError', but does not enumerate the upstream consumer of get_parent_map nor confirm it tolerates/handles the now-propagating error (whether it aborts the reconciler cleanly, is logged, or crashes uncaught).
scenarios: A stall now raises RunawayPaginationError out of get_parent_map; the caller had no handler for it (it only expected {}), so reconciliation aborts with an uninstrumented traceback
findings.suggested_fix: Add a sentence identifying get_parent_map's caller and state that the propagated error is logged at the boundary (or cite the reader that already re-raises past fail-open), consistent with acli_graph.py:304-306.

findings.checklist_item: Enumerate the three `fetcher.fetch_snapshot` fail-open consumers (fetcher.py:610, 652, 688) as edit targets requiring an `except RunawayPaginationError: raise` clause (mirroring acli_graph.py:304/394/477), so the stall error is not swallowed for get_parent_map/get_comment_map/get_issuelinks_map on the production path.
evidence: fetcher.py:586-615 wraps get_parent_map in `except Exception: warn; degraded snapshot` (line 610)
fetcher.py:631-657 wraps get_comment_map in `except Exception: warn; per-ticket fallback` (line 652)
fetcher.py:668-690 wraps get_issuelinks_map in `except Exception: warn; degraded snapshot` (line 688)
Cited authority `acli_graph.py` re-raises RunawayPaginationError at THREE sites (304, 394, 477), one per whole-project reader, precisely because each has its own fail-open handler
RunawayPaginationError is defined `class RunawayPaginationError(RuntimeError)` (acli_graph.py:29) and the plan step 1 makes the DC one likewise a RuntimeError — caught by a bare `except Exception`
findings.finding: The plan enumerates only ONE fail-open consumer (`_hierarchy.py`'s `get_parent_map`) but `_paged_search` feeds THREE whole-project readers, and all three are consumed by `fetcher.fetch_snapshot`, whose broad `except Exception` handlers (fetcher.py:610 parent, 652 comment, 688 issuelink) will silently swallow the new `RunawayPaginationError` (a RuntimeError, hence an Exception).
findings.location: Plan §Plan step 2 and §Plan scope statement ('the diff touches only the guard, its one re-raise, the facade re-export, and the test'); AC line 2
scenarios: An offset-blind DC instance spins on get_comment_map or get_issuelinks_map during a real reconcile pass; the stall error is raised by _paged_search but caught at fetcher.py:652/688 and degraded to a partial comment/link map — the exact silent-loss outcome the fix targets
get_parent_map: even with the planned _hierarchy.py re-raise, the escaped error hits fetcher.py:610 and is swallowed, so the 'loud' contract never reaches the production path
findings.suggested_fix: Add `except RunawayPaginationError: raise` ahead of the broad `except Exception` at fetcher.py:610, 652, and 688 (and import/re-export the error so fetcher can name it), matching the Cloud sibling's three re-raise sites; widen the plan scope statement and AC2 accordingly.

findings.checklist_item: Correct the scope statement to acknowledge the fetcher.py consumer edits (three re-raise clauses) rather than 'its one re-raise', or justify why fetcher's fail-open swallow is acceptable/out-of-scope.
evidence: Only _hierarchy.py:91 is a fail-open handler INSIDE the adapter dir; fetcher.py's three handlers are OUTSIDE adapters/jira_datacenter
The plan's own AC4 references 'all three whole-project readers', acknowledging three readers, yet the guard-propagation plan addresses only one handler
findings.finding: The plan's scope statement asserts the edit-set is exhaustive ('touches only the guard, its one re-raise, the facade re-export, and the test'), but this under-counts the fail-open sites: there are three production fail-open handlers in fetcher.py plus the one in _hierarchy.py, so 'its one re-raise' is an inaccurate blast-radius claim.
findings.location: Plan §Plan (scope statement: 'Deliberately narrow ... the diff touches only the guard, its one re-raise, the facade re-export, and the test')
scenarios: A reviewer or implementer trusts the 'deliberately narrow' scope claim and ships without touching fetcher.py, leaving two of three readers unguarded on the production path

findings.checklist_item: Confirm the local `RunawayPaginationError` is the intended tradeoff over reusing the sibling error type (vs. importing acli_graph's or a shared family error), and if kept local, mirror its base class, message shape, and rebar-ticket citation so all three sibling stall errors stay recognisably the same defect class.
evidence: Plan: 'define RunawayPaginationError(RuntimeError) beside the pager (local to the DC adapter, no cross-adapter coupling to Cloud's acli_graph)' — affirmative reasoning present, so NIH is not asserted
acli_graph.py:29 `class RunawayPaginationError(RuntimeError)` — identical name, base, and same-page-twice semantics in the Cloud sibling
fetcher.py:102 `class SilentTruncationError` carries `reason='offset-stall'` (fetcher.py:337-343) for the same offset-stall case on the parallel surface
Plan: 'Same defect class as cabc ... and fetcher._iter_pages' — the plan itself frames all three as one class
findings.finding: The plan introduces a third distinctly-named stall error (`RunawayPaginationError` local to `_base.py`) for a defect class it itself asserts is identical across three surfaces, while the codebase already has `acli_graph.RunawayPaginationError` (same name/base/semantics) and `fetcher.SilentTruncationError(reason='offset-stall')`. The plan gives affirmative reasoning (avoid cross-adapter DC->Cloud coupling), so this is not asserted NIH — but the naming/sharing tradeoff is worth an explicit confirmation so the DC error is at least consistent with its siblings.
scenarios: A future maintainer greps for the stall-error type across adapters and finds three different classes/messages for one defect class, making the shared contract harder to reason about

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify that the first-key repeat check excludes a None/absent first key before comparing (mirror acli_graph.py:334's `if first_key is not None and first_key == prev_first_key`), so keyless pages neither spuriously fire nor silently defeat the guard.
evidence: Plan step 1: 'remember the previous page's first issue key; if a page repeats it, raise'
Sibling authority acli_graph.py:334 guards `if first_key is not None and first_key == prev_first_key` — the None case is explicitly excluded before comparison
_hierarchy.py:81-83 shows issues without a 'key' are a real, handled case (`key = issue.get('key'); if not key: continue`), so keyless/None first-key pages can occur
findings.finding: The guard mechanism as described ('remember the previous page's first issue key; if a page repeats it, raise') does not specify how a missing/None first-issue key is handled, so two consecutive keyless pages could either spuriously fire (None == None) or silently defeat the guard.
scenarios: A page whose first unwrapped issue lacks a 'key' field is served twice consecutively
An offset-blind server that returns keyless payloads at every offset
findings.suggested_fix: In step 1, state the guard compares only non-None first keys: capture `first_key = batch[0].get('key')` and raise only when `first_key is not None and first_key == prev_first_key`, matching the sibling at acli_graph.py:334.
